alert.label: Travel update
alert.grishma: Grishma — hot days: start outdoor plans early and carry water. Mango season in Rajshahi.
alert.barsha: Barsha — haors are full and houseboats are running. Check the weather before boat trips.
alert.sharat: Sharat — clear skies and kash flowers on the char lands. Best light for photos.
alert.hemanta: Hemanta — harvest season: golden paddy, calm water and pleasant days.
alert.sheet: Sheet — dense morning fog can delay ferries and buses. Leave buffer time.
alert.basanta: Basanta — shimul and palash are in bloom. Popular spots get crowded on weekends.

tagline.grishma: Mango orchards, kalbaishakhi storms and empty beaches.
tagline.barsha: The haors become inland seas and the waterfalls wake up.
tagline.sharat: White kash flowers, blue skies and shapla-filled beels.
tagline.hemanta: Golden paddy, harvest festivals and calm water.
tagline.sheet: Morning fog, migratory birds and date-palm juice at dawn.
tagline.basanta: Shimul and palash turn the countryside red.

intro.grishma: Pohela Boishakh opens the year with fairs across the country. Days are hot, so travel early and late: terracotta temples and old capitals glow at golden hour, Rajshahi and Chapainawabganj fill with mangoes, and the coast is quiet and cheap before the monsoon.
intro.barsha: Rain changes the map. Tanguar and Hakaluki haors flood into open water you cross by houseboat, Ratargul’s trees stand in the water, and the hill-tract waterfalls run at full power. Check the weather before boat trips and keep plans flexible.
intro.sharat: The rain stops and the sky clears. Char lands along the Jamuna and Padma fill with white kash, shapla lilies cover the beels at dawn, and Durga Puja lights up towns and villages. Water is still high, so haor and river trips are at their most beautiful.
intro.hemanta: Harvest season: paddy turns gold, villages celebrate Nabanna, and the weather is pleasant almost everywhere. Hill roads are dry again, tea gardens are green, and it is the start of the main travel season, so book stays early for long weekends.
intro.sheet: Peak season. Migratory birds arrive on the haors and beels, the Sundarbans and Saint Martin’s open for cruises, and villages tap khejur rosh before sunrise. Dense fog can delay ferries and buses in the morning; leave buffer time.
intro.basanta: Pohela Falgun brings yellow saris and flower fairs. Shimul and palash bloom across the north-east, Shimul Bagan in Sunamganj turns red, and days are warm and dry. Popular spots get crowded on weekends.

intro.haor: In the monsoon the haors of the north-east flood into inland seas you cross by houseboat; in winter they shrink into grasslands full of migratory birds. Go for sunsets on the water, swamp forests and nights on deck.
intro.hill: The Chittagong Hill Tracts and the Sylhet borderlands rise into ridges, cloud valleys and indigenous villages. Most treks need a local guide and some need permits; the dry months from October to March are the easiest.
intro.river: Bangladesh is a delta of more than 700 rivers. Ride a launch, drift past floating markets, watch fishermen at dawn or follow a clear hill river over its stones.
intro.waterfall: Waterfalls are at their fullest in the monsoon and right after it. Trails get slippery, so go with a guide, start early and check the weather the day before.
intro.garden: Rolling tea estates, rubber and lemon gardens, and quiet green parks. Mornings are best, when mist sits between the bushes and the pickers are out.
intro.heritage: Buddhist monasteries, terracotta temples, sultanate mosques, zamindar palaces and Mughal forts. Two of Bangladesh’s three UNESCO World Heritage Sites are here.
intro.other: Markets, museums, viewpoints, parks and local favourites that do not fit one box but are worth the detour.
